newsitem.title: USA: Dade County, Fla., solid waste revs Baa1 - Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Dade County, Fla., solid waste revs Baa1 - Moody's.

text.p: Effective November 19, 1996, Moody's has confirmed the Baa1 rating on the Dade County Solid Waste System revenue bonds.
The system consists of an integrated solid waste network including collection, and disposal activities, landfill operations and a resource recovery facility.
Between 1991-95, system waste tonnage declined from 2.3 million to 1.3 million due largely to uncompetitive tip fees, causing various fiscal pressures.
Consequently, Moody's downgraded the rating from A to Baa1.
However, in January 1996, the county implemented structural changes that, among other factors, should provide a steady waste stream and financial stability.

Unaudited figures for fiscal year 1996 suggest that the system performance is improving and if these changes are sustained, then the credit quality should strengthen. Lower Tip Fees Improve System's Competitive Position
The county has lowered the tip fee per ton from $59 to $45, making the system more competitive with neighboring facilities, a credit strength.
The fee is fixed for three years, and can only be adjusted by the rate of inflation, capped at 5%, thereafter. Contractual Agreements Should Provide Stable Waste Stream
The lower tip fee has enticed local muncipalities and haulers to sign long- term contracts to deliver their waste to county facilties.

These contracts, along with the county's own collection efforts, increase commited waste to 90% for 1997, up from about 40% in 1991. Projections for revenue waste are stable at 1.5 million tons and assumptions appear conservative. In a couple of years, however, the county must deliver between 1.2 million and 1.4 million tons of waste to its vendors. Any shortfall in waste delivered to its facilities, therefore, would cause credit concerns. County Diversifying Revenue Stream and Adding Some Financial Flexibililty

The county is also diversifying its revenue stream. It will receive revenue from a portion of the utility service fee, and has introduced a disposal fee on haulers in the unicorporated area of the county.

Expenses are fixed, according to officials, and advance at a 2.6% rate per year. Officials can adjust the various fees to increase revenues if necessary, providing some financial flexibility. No Major Capital Needs Anticipated

Other than landfill closures and completion of its current projects, the county has limited solid waste capital needs. Debt service coverage is forecasted to drop to 1.43 times, in fact, from the current level 2.8 times (1996, unaudited), but then hovers around 1.8 times by 2003. Also, with this refunding, the county has changed some legal provisions. However, none of the changes alter credit quality.
